DNS Tunnelling 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertSuspicious DNS activity - possible DNS tunnelling / C2 beaconing. An internal host is making a steady stream of DNS queries to a single unfamiliar domain. Every query name carries an unusually long, random-looking subdomain, and the queries repeat at a regular short interval for several minutes.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know which machine was talking to whom, how often, and for how long.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

DNSThe system that turns names into addresses: www.microsoft.com becomes an IP number. Every lookup is a DNS query, and almost all of them leave your network.
Registered domainThe base part of a name, once the subdomain is stripped off. In cdn.jsdelivr.net it is jsdelivr.net. Its field is dns.question.registered_domain.
SubdomainEverything in front of the base part — the cdn there, or the www in www.microsoft.com. Its field is dns.question.subdomain.
A record / TXT recordThe two kinds of question DNS is normally asked. A means “give me an address”; TXT means “give me a piece of text”. Attackers lean on TXT because it can carry data both ways.
DNS tunnellingCarrying data out of the network inside DNS query names. DNS is almost always allowed outbound, so it is the one channel an attacker can rely on. That is the attack in this lab.
C2 beaconingCommand and control. A compromised machine calling home on a timer, over and over, and taking instructions in the reply.
Beacon intervalThe regular gap between those calls. Clockwork timing is the signal — people and normal software are irregular.
ResolverThe internal server that does the looking up on your behalf, on port 53. In this lab every single C2 query went to one resolver and nowhere else.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
Index / data viewOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* (sign-ins) and dns-* (name lookups). In Kibana this is called a data view.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 241 in the auth-* pile and 179 in dns-*. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana’s search bar. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. a domain name, an IP address, a host.
True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The four fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by four fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • dns.question.registered_domain — the base part of a name. All the beacon traffic to one domain is one value of this field, and that is what makes it easy to isolate.
  • dns.question.subdomain — the label in front of it. A long run of random letters here is the giveaway.
  • source.ip — which internal host asked the question. Your pivot field.
  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record in the auth-* pile. You only need two of them: 4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4688 = a program was started
The shape of the attack, before you see it

DNS tunnelling always has the same beats: one host asks one unfamiliar domain many times in a short window, every name is different, and the gaps are identical. Any one of those five facts on its own is unremarkable. Hold the pattern in your head — by the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it, and you will be able to say which of the five you have actually proved.

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification every document in the auth data view = 241 every document in the dns data view = 179 query 1 every successful logon = 52 query 2 the dns baseline = 179 query 3 the beacon, and the rule query = 50 query 4 the beacon from one host = 50 query 5 the one logon on that host = 1 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "dns" index pattern dns-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address” and “dns.question.name holds an exact keyword” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 50 of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Look at the Severity column. Every row says critical. Look at Risk Score beside it: 99.
  2. Find the count just above the table, next to Columns. It says 50 alerts. That is fifty separate events, not one summary.
  3. Look at the Top alerts by host.name panel. It says sec-win-05, 100%. Write that host name down.
  4. Read the Reason column on any row. It tells you the records came from 10.0.4.13 and went to 10.0.4.10:53.
Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September at 10:02 UTC, which is the morning of the attack. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. The alert carries two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-30T10:56:15.074Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:02:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules; ours is the only one you have, so it sits under Custom rules. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Click the rule called Burst of DNS queries with long encoded subdomains to one unfamiliar domain.
  3. Read its Custom query. It is dns.question.registered_domain: "exfil-c2.example" — character for character the query you will type yourself in a few cards.
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your own query count have to agree. The rule says 50, so when query 3 later returns 50 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The fifty alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, fifty critical alerts, risk score 99, all raised from records on 10.0.4.13 / sec-win-05, all going to the resolver on port 53. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the shape of the attack: one machine, one destination, a great many events.

Your browser just opened. Here is where you are.

no typing needed

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — the attack is over a week old and Discover is looking at the last few minutes, so it is simply showing you nothing yet. Here is the real screen, exactly as you are looking at it now:

Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

This build of Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language, and the Try ES|QL button is an advert for it aimed at people who already know their way around. If you click it you will land on a screen showing this:

The error you will seeFROM logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-* | WHERE @timestamp >= ?_tstart AND @timestamp <= ?_tend | LIMIT 10 Unknown index [logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-*]

That query looks for indices called logs-* and filebeat-*. Our lab has no such indices — it has auth-* and dns-*. So the query cannot work and that error is expected. It does not mean the lab is broken, and there is nothing for you to fix.

What to do instead: press the browser’s Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

And do not type in the dark bar at the very top

The box labelled Find apps, content, and more in the black bar searches Kibana’s own navigation, not your logs. Your data is searched in the big white box a little lower down. They look similar and they are not, and typing your query into the wrong one is the second most common stumble in this lab.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is fine, the search bar is fine, Kibana is healthy. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. The next two cards make you do the same thing by hand, so you can pick the right pile and pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?3 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search row — the control with the label Data view beside it. It reads auth-*.
  2. Look at the list that opens. There are only two entries that are yours, and this is what it looks like:
  1. Click dns-*.
The two entries that matter, and what is in them
Data viewDocumentsHolds
auth-*241Windows security events: successful logons, logoffs, failures, lockouts, privilege assignments, Kerberos failures, process starts
dns-*179Name lookups: the name that was asked, its registered domain and subdomain, the query type, the response code, and the source and destination addresses and ports

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so a single entry covers every day of auth logs. If you ever see a third entry here that you do not recognise, leave it alone and pick dns-*.

You will still see no documents after closing this panel. That is correct — the time range is still the last 15 minutes. The next card fixes that.

Why this matters

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the sidebar says “no available fields” and stays that way

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

If you would rather pin the exact day by hand

Both methods give the same 179 documents, because every record in this lab happened inside 22 September 2026. But if you want a fixed window you can type yourself, click the left half of the time range and the absolute editor opens:

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC, and every picture in this guide was taken on a computer set to UTC+8. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your own computer’s timezone, and no setting inside Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours behind UTC, the first beacon that this guide calls Sep 22, 2026 @ 10:02:00.000 will appear in your table as Sep 22, 2026 @ 02:02:00.000.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 2 minutes, then 12, 12, 12 — are identical in every timezone on earth.
  • The gaps are the evidence. The beacon runs for 9 minutes 48 seconds. The sign-in is 2 minutes before the first beacon. Write those down and you are right in any timezone.

Here is the one table you need if you want to convert a time this guide quotes. Find your own offset, then add or subtract it:

Your computer isExample citiesThen 10:02:00 UTC shows as
UTC+0Lagos, London in winterSep 22 @ 10:02:00
UTC+1Berlin, Paris, MadridSep 22 @ 11:02:00
UTC+2Cairo, Helsinki, JohannesburgSep 22 @ 12:02:00
UTC+5:30India, ColomboSep 22 @ 15:32:00
UTC+8Singapore, Beijing, Perth, Kuala LumpurSep 22 @ 18:02:00
UTC+9Tokyo, SeoulSep 22 @ 19:02:00
UTC−5New York, TorontoSep 22 @ 05:02:00
UTC−6Chicago, Mexico CitySep 22 @ 04:02:00
UTC−8Los Angeles, VancouverSep 22 @ 02:02:00

Not sure what your offset is? Look at the first bar of your histogram and compare it with the 00:00 printed under the left edge. Whatever the difference is, that is your offset. Or simply set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start — then every picture in this guide matches your screen exactly. Not required. But it removes a whole category of confusion.

  • The sidebar lists 20 available fields with a coloured badge beside each one. Those badges tell you what each field can be asked to do, and they are the same badges you will see on every field panel from here on.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just click Search entire time range again. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Investigate7

Query 1 — every successful logon that day

1 of 5 queries3 min
Why you are running this query

Before you can say something is unusual, you have to know what normal looks like. 4624 is the record written every time any account signs in successfully, and in a real Windows estate it is one of the most common records there is.

So this query deliberately produces a number that tells you nothing. Running it teaches you something worth more than the number: an event code on its own is not a finding.

Do this

  1. Switch the Data view on the far left to auth-*. It is the dropdown you opened two cards ago.
  2. Click inside the search bar, select whatever is in it, and paste in exactly this — then press Enter:
Search 1 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success"
What 52 actually tells you

52 accounts signed in successfully across the whole estate that day, and they are smeared evenly from one end of the day to the other. There is no cluster, nothing at any particular moment.

That is exactly what healthy sign-in traffic looks like: ordinary people starting their working day. If you stop here and write “sign-in activity looks normal”, you will be right, and you will also have found nothing.

What to do next, and why

You cannot see a shape inside a smear. To find the cluster you have to stop counting everybody and start counting one machine at a time — and the alert has already told you which one, on the Top alerts by host.name panel.

The card after this one, The dead end, closes off 52 for good by counting its distinct values. Then Query 2 goes back to the DNS pile, where the attack actually is.

Dead end8

Prove the dead end: break the 52 down

one field panel4 min

Before moving on, let us be certain that 52 really is a dead end. There is one click that answers “how is this result set spread out?”, and every analyst uses it before trusting any count.

Do this

  1. Leave the search bar exactly as it is: event.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success".
  2. In the left sidebar, under Available fields, click host.name. A panel opens over the results.
  3. Read the four values and the four percentages. Write the smallest one down.
The number that closes the dead end

Read these off the panel and write them down. They are why Query 1 cannot answer the question:

HostShare of the 52What it means
sec-win-0140.4%21 sign-ins on one busy workstation
sec-win-0328.8%15 sign-ins
sec-win-0428.8%15 sign-ins
sec-win-051.9%exactly one sign-in, and it is the machine from the alert

Four ordinary machines, smeared over a whole day. That is a normal Tuesday. There is nothing here to escalate, and no amount of staring at these 52 records will produce something that is not there.

Notice the shape of the trap, because it is the shape of half of all bad alert analysis: 52 is a big number, and it means nothing.

Why a dead end is the most useful card in this lab

Almost every bad alert triage in the real world dies right here. Somebody queries the scary event, gets a large number, and then either panics and escalates noise, or shrugs and closes a real incident. Both are mistakes, and both come from stopping at this screen.

You now know what “a normal day of sign-ins” looks like, because you have seen it counted. That is a baseline, and you cannot spot an anomaly without one. And you have noted that the loneliest row in the whole table is the machine the alert named — which is only visible because you broke the number down.

What to do next, and why

Two of the five facts of a beacon you already have from the alert page: one machine and one unfamiliar domain. The remaining three — many queries, every name different, identical gaps — are all in the dns-* pile, which is where the rest of this lab lives.

Narrow it9

Query 2 — all 179 DNS queries, and the one that does not belong

2 of 5 queries4 min
Why the baseline comes before the hunt

You cannot recognise an odd thing until you know what the ordinary thing looks like on this estate. And here is the good news: the data names the attacker’s domain for you. Nothing on this card is a filter you invented — you are reading a ranked list and noticing that one row does not belong.

Do this

  1. Switch the Data view to dns-* again, and clear the search box completely. An empty box means everything; you can also type *.
  2. Leave the time range alone. It is still covering the whole day.
  3. Now click dns.question.registered_domain in the left column, under Available fields. A panel opens over the results showing the most common values with a percentage bar on each. Read them from the top down.
What you have just found

One domain takes 27.9% of every DNS query on the estate — roughly one query in every four. The next busiest takes 6.7%. That is more than four times everything else combined, and out of only 16 distinct domains, so this is not merely “the busiest site”.

Write the domain down. You found it; this guide did not tell you.

Why a busy site does not explain this

A genuinely popular internal site would be popular; that is what popular means. What gives this one away is the name and the shape together:

  • You do not recognise it, and nothing on a normal estate generates four times its nearest rival’s traffic by accident.
  • Its ending is .example, which is reserved by the IETF (RFC 2606) precisely so it can never be registered on the public internet. It cannot be a real business’s site. It cannot be anything except something somebody made for this.
  • It does not sound like a company either. exfil and c2 are the two words a defender uses for this exact technique, and attackers who name their infrastructure like this are usually writing for the attention of exactly the person reading this card.

One caution about wording, because it matters in a report: that percentage is a share of queries, not of hosts and not of bytes. Never report it as “28% of the network”.

What to do next, and why

You have a domain. Put it in a filter and everything about the attack becomes countable. That is the next card, and it is the breakthrough of this lab.

Narrow it10

Query 3 — isolate the beacon

3 of 5 queries4 min
The one filter the alert was written to be found by

Turn 179 mixed queries into only the suspicious ones, and count them. This is the breakthrough, and it is a single line of text — and it is the same line the detection rule runs, so the count you are about to read has to be the same as the 50 alerts on the page you started from.

Do this

  1. Clear the search box, then type the filter below. Keep the quotation marks — a missing closing quote is the usual cause of a red error.
  2. Press Enter.
Search 3 — type this, then press Enterdns.question.registered_domain: "exfil-c2.example"

dns.question.registered_domain is the base part of each name, stripped of its subdomain. Quoting it means “exactly this word, nothing else”.

Fifty, in under ten minutes of the day

Every one of those 50 queries happened inside a single nine-minute block. The rest of the day, which was a steady trickle, is now completely empty. The alert’s shape — “several minutes, not all day” — is now visible as one block of bars you could put a finger on.

Two facts, and only two, are proved so far: 50 queries, and all of them to one unfamiliar domain. The next three cards turn those into the other three facts of the pattern.

Get the count off the tab, and know where it lives

There is no separate counter box to misread. The count is part of the tab’s own name: Documents (50). That is the number you quote in your report, and the number your instructor will check.

Do not clear this filter for the next four cards

Every number from here until the last query means “of these 50”. If you accidentally empty the search box you are back to 179 and the counts stop meaning anything. It is the single easiest mistake to make in a lab like this.

Narrow it11

Query 4 — how many machines, sockets and destinations?

4 of 5 queries5 min
Why the number of hosts changes everything

One compromised machine is a contained incident you can isolate tonight. Fifty is a breach of the whole subnet. You cannot answer that without this card — and you cannot scope the response without the other two numbers that come with it.

Do this — three parts

  1. Leave the filter from the last card exactly as it is, on the Documents tab.
  2. In the left sidebar, click source.ip — “the address that asked the question”. Read the panel.
  3. Then make the filter say it too. Add the address to the search bar and press Enter:
Search 4 — type this, then press Enterdns.question.registered_domain: "exfil-c2.example" and source.ip: "10.0.4.13"
One host. All fifty. Not one straggler.

Not one of the 50 came from anywhere else, and adding the clause to the query changed the count by nothing at all — still Documents (50). That is a much stronger sentence than “there was one IP”: it means the beacon and the host are the same set of records.

This is not a botnet and not a many-host campaign. It is a single machine, and that is the sentence your report leads with.

One host, one port, one program — go and prove the port bit

Click the Field statistics tab, immediately to the right of Documents (50). It is a tab, not a panel further down the page. Look at two rows there:

  • source.port — 1 distinct value, 54744.
  • host.name — 1 distinct value, sec-win-05.

A person opening a tool fifty times would get a new random source port every time. One port, reused on a fixed schedule for the whole run, is a program holding a socket open. That is a far stronger sentence than “there was one IP”, and you can defend every word of it with a cell in that table.

And where did the data go?

Same table: destination.ip has 1 distinct value (10.0.4.10), and destination.port is drawn as 1 value (53). Port 53 is DNS. Every one of those 50 queries went to your internal resolver and nowhere else.

That is exactly what tunnelling looks like from the network’s point of view: the exfiltration rides the resolver, so on the wire it is indistinguishable from ordinary name resolution. Nothing about it would trigger a firewall rule, which is the whole reason this technique works.

Count it12

Fifty queries, fifty different names. Not one repeated.

the other tab4 min

Everything so far has been counts and percentages. This card is where the attack stops being a shape and becomes arithmetic nobody can argue with: 50 records, 50 distinct values, and a label length with no overlap with anything else on the estate.

Do this

  1. Keep the search bar as it is, and stay on the dns-* data view.
  2. Click the Field statistics tab, next to Documents (50).
  3. Read the Distinct values column. It is the fourth column, after Type, Name and Documents (%).
Fifty queries, fifty different names, and why TXT matters

Read those rows together and you have something no amount of “lots of queries” can give you: a brand new name every single time, and nothing ever reused.

  • Every query succeeded. NOERROR on all 50 means the tunnel was working the whole time. There is no failed attempt to explain away and no sign of an attacker trying and giving up.
  • A third of them were TXT records — 17 of 50. A TXT record asks for a piece of text back. Ordinary name resolution almost never needs one. TXT records are how a tunneller carries data in both directions: out in the query name, and back in the answer.
Compare that with the baseline, because this is the whole argument

Go back to the 179-query baseline for a moment. Across the whole day on this estate, dns.question.name has only 96 distinct values — 179 requests reusing 96 names, because the same www.microsoft.com gets asked over and over all day. That is what real DNS does.

This traffic does the exact opposite, in the most extreme way available: a fresh name every time, over a short period, from one machine. Nobody types a random string fifty times. Something is generating them — and generating them is the only reason they need to be new, because each one carries a different piece of data out with it.

Now the length, and the reason it needs no argument

Click dns.question.subdomain in the left column and read the values in the panel. Every label is a long run of random letters and digits — 44 characters — far longer than any name a person or a normal application would choose.

And here is the part that makes it a finding rather than an opinion: the longest subdomain anywhere in the other 129 queries is 10 characters. 44 against 10. There is nothing in between, so you never have to argue about where the threshold should be — the two populations simply do not overlap. A threshold-based rule here would have been a judgement call; this is arithmetic.

Get the detail13

Open one document and read all of it

the right button4 min

The table shows you a summary. For the exact values — and for the one field the summary hides — you need to open a record. The record worth opening is the last one, because it is the odd one out.

Never click the row. Click the little arrows.

Each row has a small button with two arrows pointing diagonally away from each other, in a narrow column immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. Click that. Clicking anywhere else in the row does nothing at all — this is the single most common stumble in this lab, and it makes people think the lab is broken.

Do this

  1. Go back to the Documents tab. The newest record is the last beacon, at 10:11:48.000Z.
  2. Click the ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button at the far left of that row.
  3. In the panel that opens, click the JSON tab, next to Table. The JSON view prints the stored values exactly, with no formatting and no timezone conversion.
Three things to notice, in this one record
  • The name is enormous. Roughly twice the length of every other one in the run, and the only record where network.bytes goes to 168 instead of 96. The last query being the biggest is the signature of a transfer finishing — the machine flushed the rest of what it was holding and then stopped.
  • The timestamp ends in Z. That is UTC, written exactly as stored: 2026-09-22T10:11:48.000Z. Compare it with the same record in the Table view, which draws it eight hours later because of the timezone on the machine that took this picture. This is the one place you can always read a time that needs no caveat.
  • One socket, one host, one destination. host.name is sec-win-05, source.ip is 10.0.4.13 and the destination is 10.0.4.10 on port 53. One program, talking to the resolver, on a loop.
Getting back to the table

Click Close at the bottom of the panel, or the × at its top right, or just press Escape. Your filters and your scroll position stay exactly as they were.

The clock14

The clock, which is what makes it a beacon

the fifth fact4 min
Why timing, and not just volume

Fifty queries across a whole day is nothing — this estate made 129 ordinary ones. Fifty queries packed into a few minutes on a fixed timer is a machine. The count tells you how much left the network; the interval tells you it was automated, and that is the difference between a compromise and a curiosity.

Do this

  1. Still on the Query 4 filter, on the Documents tab. Close the document panel first if it is still open.
  2. Read the newest row — that is the last beacon. Write the timestamp down exactly as shown.
  3. Read the three or four rows immediately below it, and subtract. Then find the oldest row: click the @timestamp column heading to reverse the sort, and read the top row.
If you want the number rather than the impression

You have a count N, a first time and a last time. Divide the span by N minus one — the first query starts the clock and does not consume a gap:

The arithmeticinterval = (last timestamp - first timestamp) / (N - 1)

For this data that is 588 seconds / 49 gaps = 12 seconds, and it lands on a whole number with no remainder at all. That is the whole test, and it is worth understanding rather than skipping:

  • Divides exactly → clockwork. A timer, and the beacon signature.
  • Awkward remainder, or visibly different gaps → human browsing, or retry logic. Not a beacon.

And the total span: 588 seconds is 9 minutes 48 seconds. Not ten minutes “or so” — a number you can put in a report.

Write the times in the form your report needs
  1. Say which zone the times are in. “18:02” on its own is not a fact — it is a fact plus an assumption. Write “18:02 local (10:02 UTC)”, or state your zone once above the table.
  2. If you use the data’s own values, label them UTC explicitly.
  3. Lead with the interval. “one query every 12 seconds, with no exceptions, for 9 minutes 48 seconds” is true in every timezone on earth and needs no conversion at all.
Why gaps are the durable finding

Every absolute time you write will be wrong for a reader in another time zone. Every interval is correct everywhere. So “it ran 9 minutes 48 seconds at a fixed 12-second interval” is the claim that survives contact with somebody else’s screen — and it is one of the ones that establishes this was automated rather than hurried.

Close it15

Query 5 — the same dead end from card 8, done properly

5 of 5 queries4 min
This is the payoff for narrowing

Card 8 ran a query and got a useless 52. This is the same query with one clause added, and it returns one. Everything you need to open your timeline is in that one record.

Do this

  1. Switch the Data view to auth-*.
  2. Replace the host name from card 8 into the filter below, then press Enter.
Search 5 — the card 8 query, narrowed to one hostevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success" and host.name: "sec-win-05"
One account, one logon, exactly two minutes before the first beacon

10:00:00.000Z is the very first event in this entire investigation, and the first beacon is at 10:02:00.000Z. That is a gap of exactly 2 minutes, and it is the number that makes the timeline a story instead of a list: something happened on this machine, and two minutes later the machine started talking to somebody outside.

It also hands you the two things a responder needs first: a name whose credentials to reset, and a person to ask about the phishing mail that the briefing mentions.

This logon is NOT the attack. Do not report it as one.

This is the most common beginner error in this lab. The host was already compromised before this logon — the briefing mentions a phishing attachment — and the attack is the DNS beaconing, not the sign-in.

The logon is context. It tells you who was at the keyboard while the beacon was running. Write it in a sentence that makes the difference explicit, because a reader who cannot tell them apart will assume you did not either.

Do not reach for the logon as the cause either

Nothing in the auth-* data shows how this host was actually compromised. There is not a single process-start event on it at all — the next card says so plainly. “Compromised by phishing” comes from the briefing, not from these logs. Say where each claim comes from, and a reviewer will trust the rest of it.

Know your limits16

What this lab cannot prove — and how to say so

this is expertise

You have five facts, all of them numbers, all of them pointing the same way. That is enough for a verdict. It is not enough to name a malware family, and the difference between an analyst and a guess is knowing exactly where that line is.

Three claims this data cannot support

1. You cannot name the malware, the binary or the command line

The auth-* pile does contain process-start events — event.code 4688, with process.name and process.parent.name. There are 15 of them. Every single one is on sec-win-01, sec-win-03 or sec-win-04, and not one is on sec-win-05, the beaconing host.

So there is no process record to point at, no file name, no parent process, no command line. If your report names a tool, a file or a technique that no query returned, take it out. A claim you cannot point at is worth less than no claim at all, because it is the one thing that makes a reader stop trusting the rest of the report.

2. “Compromised by phishing” is not from these logs

It comes from the briefing you were handed. That is a perfectly good source and there is nothing wrong with using it — but say so. Write “per the alert briefing, the host was previously compromised via a phishing attachment”, and then go on to say what the logs do show. An analyst who can tell those two sources apart is worth twice one who cannot.

3. “Data was exfiltrated” is an inference, and a strong one

What the logs show is 50 unique query names, 44- and 96-character random labels, a mix of TXT records, NOERROR on every one, all on a fixed 12-second timer, all from one machine to one resolver. There is no payload here to read and no byte count for the data that left.

So write “consistent with data exfiltration over DNS”, not “the attacker exfiltrated N bytes”. You can quote 168 and 96 as the query sizes, because those are real; you cannot turn them into a volume of stolen data. “Consistent with” is not a hedge — it is the most precise word the evidence actually supports.

What you can state flatly
  • One host, 10.0.4.13 / sec-win-05, asked one unfamiliar domain, exfil-c2.example, 50 times.
  • Every name was unique. The subdomain was 44 characters on 49 of them and 96 on the last, against a maximum of 10 characters anywhere else on the estate that day.
  • Every gap was exactly 12 seconds, over 9 minutes 48 seconds.
  • Every query went to one resolver on port 53, from one source port, and every one was answered NOERROR.
  • One sign-in on that host, 2 minutes before the first query.

That is a verdict. Everything in it is a number you can point at on a screen, and none of it needs a tool name, a file hash or a byte count to stand up.

Why saying “I could not prove X” makes the rest believable

Because it is the same skill as the dead end on card 8. An analyst who closes off 52 logons, closes off 129 queries from other hosts, and then writes down the three things the data cannot support is doing exactly what a careful analyst does. A report that quietly overstates is the one that gets a response team to spend a week in the wrong place.

Put it together17

Build the timeline

most important 6 min

This is the most important 6 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad or TextEdit is fine) and write five lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blank is your work — read it off your table and type it in. The gaps on the right are pre-filled, because gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. T − 2 min  →  fill in from your screen
    The baseline. A normal successful sign-in for the user mchen on sec-win-05 (10.0.4.13). Context only — not itself malicious, and the host was already compromised before it. (Query 5)
  2. T  →  first query
    The beacon begins. A DNS query to exfil-c2.example from 10.0.4.13 carrying a 44-character random subdomain, which is nothing a person or an ordinary application would ever ask for. (Query 3)
  3. T  →  last query  (50 queries)
    The run. 50 queries, one every 12 seconds with no exceptions, every name different, 33 A and 17 TXT, all NOERROR, from one source port to one resolver, spanning 9 minutes 48 seconds. (Queries 3, 4, 5, 6)
  4. T + 9:48
    One final query, roughly twice the usual size — a 96-character label, 168 bytes instead of 96. The transfer ends. (Query 7)
  5. after that
    Nothing. No more queries to that domain for the rest of the day, no second host ever joins in, and no other domain on the estate comes close to that volume. One machine, one run, then silence.

The clock times above are UTC, which is how the lab stores them and how this guide’s pictures were read. If your screen is showing a different offset, write down your numbers instead — what matters is that the five lines stay in this order and keep these gaps: 2 minutes from the sign-in to the first query, then 9 minutes 48 seconds of beaconing.

The shape of the answer

A quiet sign-in, then everything else in the lab happens inside ten minutes, in strict order: one machine, one domain, fifty identical gaps, then nothing.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, and it rules out an ordinary application doing ordinary work. Real traffic is lumpy; a timer is not.

Then ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and the query that proved it
Who started it?source.ip: 10.0.4.13  /  host.name: sec-win-05
Who was it talking to?exfil-c2.example, via the resolver at 10.0.4.10:53
How many queries?50, every 12 seconds, for 9 min 48 s
How was it done?44-character random subdomains, 50 unique names, 17 of them TXT
How far did it get?one host, one domain, one socket, one destination
Why is it not routine?nothing else on the estate produces a single 44-character label, let alone fifty
The one-sentence verdict

On 22 September 2026 a single internal workstation, 10.0.4.13 (sec-win-05), issued 50 DNS queries to the single unfamiliar domain exfil-c2.example at a fixed 12-second interval over 9 minutes 48 seconds, each query carrying a 44-character random subdomain, every name unique, 17 of them TXT queries — and then stopped.

That is a true positive. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the five queries you just ran. That is what a finished investigation looks like.

Write the report, then prove it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. Do this yourself, and do it now

Your verdict in one line

Three things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the three that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you narrow before you counted? A report that stops at “52 successful logons on the estate” is incomplete, and one that stops at “lots of DNS queries” is worse. You had to break both numbers down before either of them meant anything.
  2. Did you keep the logon and the beacon apart? The sign-in is context, not the attack. Write it as a separate timeline row and say which is which, or a reader will assume you found the entry point.
  3. Did you say what you could not prove? Three lines — no malware name, phishing from the briefing, exfiltration as an inference — are in your report. That is what makes the rest of it believable.

And one bonus: if you compared the 50 unique names against the 96 unique names across the whole day, say so. Nothing checks it automatically, but it is the single clearest sentence in the whole case.

Finish19

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container dns-tunneling-001-elasticsearch container dns-tunneling-001-kibana volume dns-tunneling-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) file .../dns-tunneling-001-/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-dns-tunneling-001-

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates, rule.json and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything, and it will not install a second copy of the detection rule.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference20

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Three things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty and there are no documents

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? It must say dns-* for the DNS cards and auth-* for the two logon cards, 7 and 15.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today while the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the fifty come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
Nothing for query 3 or 4You are on the auth-* data view. Queries 2, 3 and 4 all have to run on dns-*.
Nothing for query 5You are on the dns-* data view, or the host name in the query is not sec-win-05. Check the host.name panel on card 8 again.
17 instead of 1 for query 5You added source.ip instead of host.name, or you left the Query 4 filter in the bar. Only the two event clauses and host.name belong in this one.
49 or 51 for the subdomain countYou are reading top 10 of 50 categories off the bar chart, which is not a count. The Distinct values cell is the number that counts.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the time-range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.

3. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker Desktop is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says the engine is running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run teardown.sh (or teardown.cmd) from the folder that owns it.
a container called dns-tunneling-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run the teardown file in the old folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the dns index holds N documents but this lab ships 179A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run the setup file with reset.
the rule is installed but has not produced 50 alertsYou are on the card that matters: the alerts are not there. Run the setup file again and give it a minute — it waits for this itself. If it still fails, docker logs dns-tunneling-001-kibana says why.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value, and a field panel shows one row per value. For an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return a large number of documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of three causes, and all three are on the If it breaks card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
